trial_name: SSSP-2 — Effect of an Early Resuscitation Protocol on In-Hospital Mortality Among Adults With Sepsis and Hypotension (2017)
citation: Andrews B, Semler MW, Muchemwa L, Kelly P, Lakhi S, Heimburger DC, et al. Effect of an early resuscitation protocol on in-hospital mortality among adults with sepsis and hypotension: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2017;318(13):1233-1240.
one_liner: In adults with sepsis and hypotension in a low-resource Zambian emergency department, a protocolised 6-hour resuscitation protocol significantly increased in-hospital mortality compared with usual care (48.1% vs 33.0%).

pico.population: Adults with suspected infection, ≥2 SIRS criteria, and hypotension (SBP ≤90 mm Hg or MAP ≤65 mm Hg) in a low-resource emergency department in Zambia.
pico.intervention: Protocolised 6-hour resuscitation (2 L crystalloid in hour 1, up to 4 L by 6 h, dopamine for persistent hypotension, and PRBC transfusion for Hb <7 g/dL).
pico.comparison: Usual care determined by treating clinicians with study nurse monitoring but no mandated protocol targets.

background.existing_knowledge: Early protocolised sepsis resuscitation (fluids, vasopressors, antimicrobials) was developed and tested in high-resource systems with reliable ICU support.
background.knowledge_gap: Low-resource settings have limited ICU beds, mechanical ventilation, and monitoring, raising uncertainty about the balance between benefit and iatrogenic harm from aggressive resuscitation.
background.hypothesis: A simplified 6-hour early resuscitation protocol for adults with suspected infection and hypotension in a low-resource emergency department would reduce in-hospital mortality compared with usual care.

methods.setting: Emergency Department of University Teaching Hospital, Lusaka, Zambia; enrolled Jun 2012–Oct 2013. Only 0.5% managed in an ICU.

inclusion: Hypotension (SBP ≤90 mm Hg or MAP ≤65 mm Hg)
Enrolment within 4 h of qualifying BP and within 24 h of ED registration
exclusion: Severe hypoxaemic respiratory failure (RR >40/min and SpO2 <90%)

methods.intervention: Protocolised 6-hour resuscitation delivered by study nurse: rapid crystalloid (2 L in first hour, reassessment up to 4 L by 6 h), dopamine for persistent hypotension after fluids, and PRBC transfusion for Hb <7 g/dL. Clinical reassessments included JVP, RR, and SpO2.
methods.comparison: Usual care by treating clinicians with study nurse monitoring, without mandated targets for fluids, vasopressors, or transfusions.
methods.sample_size_power: 212 patients required to detect a 20% absolute reduction in in-hospital mortality (65% to 45%) with 80% power at 5% significance level.
secondary_outcomes: Intravenous fluid volume in first 6 h
Clinical respiratory compromise in first 6 h
methods.follow_up: In-hospital outcomes to discharge; vital status assessed to 28 days.

headline_bullets: The trial completed planned enrolment without early termination (209 analyzed of 212 randomized).
Protocolised resuscitation significantly increased in-hospital mortality (48.1% vs 33.0%, RR 1.46) and 28-day mortality (67.0% vs 45.3%, RR 1.48).
Clear exposure separation occurred in early IV fluids (median 3.5 L vs 2.0 L in 6 h) and dopamine use (14.2% vs 1.9%).
Protocol group had significantly higher early clinical respiratory compromise (35.8% vs 22.3%) despite greater 6-hour lactate reduction.

outcomes_table.note: Vital status at day 28 available for 94.2% overall
Shorter stay reflects higher early mortality in protocol group

outcomes_table.outcome: Intravenous fluid volume in first 6 h (L)

outcomes_table.note: Dopamine duration: median 4 (IQR 4–5) h vs 4 (IQR 4–4) h; P=0.52

outcomes_table.outcome: Clinical respiratory compromise in first 6 h

subgroup_table.subgroup: As-treated analysis by fluid volume (≥3 L vs <3 L)

safety: Clinical respiratory compromise in first 6 h was higher in protocol group: 35.8% vs 22.3% (P=0.03).
Iatrogenic pulmonary oedema occurred in 2/106 (1.9%) protocol patients vs 0/103 (0%) usual care patients.

domains.notes: Sequential envelopes used for allocation concealment after eligibility confirmation; baseline SAPS-3 scores were comparable (median 52 vs 54).
Open-label delivery allowed potential co-intervention and discharge bias; primary mortality endpoint is objective. Nurse monitoring in control arm created a monitored usual care condition.
3 of 212 patients excluded post-randomisation due to ineligibility (n=209 analyzed). 28-day vital status recorded in 94.2%.
Clear exposure separation in fluid volume (median 3.5 L vs 2.0 L) and dopamine (14.2% vs 1.9%). Hypotension resolution at 6 h was lower in protocol group (76.4% vs 95.1%; P<0.001).
Severely immunocompromised cohort (89.5% HIV-positive, median CD4 66–68 cells/µL, median albumin 2.1–2.3 g/dL, mean Hb 7.8 g/dL). Baseline JVP above sternal angle present in 20.8% vs 10.7%.

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is moderate due to open-label design, minor post-randomisation exclusions, and single-centre setting.

domains.notes: High-burden low-resource ED population with advanced HIV, severe anaemia, and hypoalbuminaemia; only 0.5% treated in ICU.
Highly applicable to resource-constrained settings lacking ICU and ventilatory rescue; less applicable to high-resource ICUs using norepinephrine, infusion pumps, and advanced hemodynamic monitoring.

external_validity.verdict: External validity is strong for similar low-resource emergency settings with high HIV burden, but limited for high-resource critical care environments.

strengths: First randomized trial evaluating protocolised sepsis resuscitation in a low-resource sub-Saharan ED.
Pragmatic design integrated into emergency workflow with rapid enrolment (median ~70-75 min from ED registration).
Clear separation achieved between arms for fluid and vasopressor exposures.
Objective primary endpoint with findings consistent across unadjusted, adjusted, and Cox proportional hazard models.
limitations: Single-centre, open-label trial with potential for co-intervention bias.
Observed control mortality (33.0%) was far lower than hypothesized (65%), reducing power.
Multi-component bundle prevents isolating individual effect of fluids vs dopamine vs transfusion.
Used dopamine rather than norepinephrine as the protocolised vasopressor.
Clinical volume status assessment (JVP, respiratory examination) is operator-dependent.

critical_appraisal.summary: SSSP-2 provides moderate-quality evidence that fixed-volume resuscitation protocols in low-resource settings lacking critical care rescue increase mortality.
strengths: Pragmatic RCT in an underrepresented population
Consistent harm signal across all analytical models
weaknesses: Inability to isolate single intervention component

sections.authors_conclusion: In adults with sepsis and hypotension in a low-resource Zambian emergency department, a simplified 6-hour resuscitation protocol increased in-hospital mortality compared with usual care.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Do not implement rigid fixed-volume resuscitation protocols in low-resource settings without critical care backup; individualized frequent reassessment is essential.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult ED patients with sepsis and hypotension in low-resource health systems with high HIV prevalence and limited ICU capacity.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Resuscitation fluids and vasopressors should be withheld entirely in resource-limited settings.
implementation_caveats: Fixed fluid boluses (2–4 L) without ventilatory backup risk iatrogenic pulmonary oedema.
Dopamine is no longer first-line vasopressor in modern practice.
Biochemical improvements (e.g., lactate clearance) do not guarantee survival benefit.

controversies.notes: Aggressive fluid protocols increase mortality when ventilatory support and critical care rescue are unavailable to treat fluid overload.
Debate exists over whether fluid volume, dopamine toxicity, or delayed antibiotics drove harm; trialists noted antibiotic timing was identical between groups.
Protocol improved 6-hour lactate clearance (−1.2 vs −0.5 mmol/L) yet increased mortality, proving biochemical markers are unreliable surrogates for outcome.

context_related_trials.relation: Supported fluid-sparing strategies and caution with liberal early fluids in ICU sepsis.
Demonstrated equivalent outcomes between restrictive and liberal fluid strategies in early septic shock.

unresolved_questions: What is the optimal fluid volume and vasopressor threshold in low-resource settings lacking mechanical ventilation?
Which specific protocol element (fluids vs dopamine) contributed most to the excess mortality?

numbers_to_remember: In-hospital mortality: 48.1% protocol vs 33.0% control (RR 1.46, P=0.03)
IV fluid in first 6 h: median 3.5 L vs 2.0 L (P<0.001)
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: In low-resource settings lacking ICU backup, rigid early fluid/vasopressor protocols increase mortality despite improving lactate clearance.
